item.title: Mobavenue’s Tejas Rathod On The Shift From Ad Optimisation To AI Decisioning
item.dc:creator: Inc42 Staff
item.description: A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app…
item.content:encoded:
A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app does not promise a purchase. Yet these remain the metrics that digital advertising has traditionally been built around.

For brands, the real challenge is understanding whether a click or app download will actually translate into a business outcome. As advertisers demand clearer links between media spending and business outcomes, adtech is moving towards systems that can predict intent, learn from downstream behaviour and optimise for what happens beyond the click or install.

This is the shift Mobavenue is targeting. The company processes more than 1.25 Bn data signals a day and has built its technology stack around real-time decisioning and continuous feedback from campaign outcomes. In FY26, it delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, giving its models a growing base of data to learn from.

At the centre of this is Mobavenue’s Neural Engine, which connects signals, intent and outcomes. Rather than treating a bid, click or install as the endpoint, the system is designed to learn from what happens after that decision and use those outcomes to inform future audience, bidding and budget decisions.

For Tejas Rathod, founder and CTO of Mobavenue, this marks a broader shift in advertising — from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across the marketing lifecycle.

In a conversation with Inc42, Rathod explains the technology behind Mobavenue’s platform, how the company approaches privacy and invalid traffic, and why it is building towards an advertising ecosystem that connects awareness, acquisition and activation. 

Here are the edited excerpts…

Inc42: What has been the biggest shift in the Digital advertising industry, and what is driving it?

Tejas Rathod: The biggest shift is the movement from automation towards predictive intelligence and AI autonomy. Earlier, technology helped advertisers execute decisions faster. Today, AI is increasingly being used to anticipate intent, learn from outcomes and make decisions dynamically.

This is being driven by the growing complexity of digital ecosystems, the volume of signals available and the pressure to deliver measurable business outcomes. The next phase is moving from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as an increasingly autonomous decision-making layer.

Inc42: With privacy regulations tightening and invalid traffic remaining a challenge, how has Mobavenue prepared its tech to maintain targeting accuracy and campaign efficiency? 

Tejas Rathod: Privacy has been a foundational consideration in how we have built our tech. Our platforms operate within the requirements of applicable privacy frameworks and regulations across the markets we serve, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework. We also use privacy-conscious approaches to identity, including ID masking and hashing, to derive intelligence without unnecessarily exposing identifiable information.

Our models rely on aggregated, consented signals and behavioural patterns. This lets the system understand user intent and quality while maintaining data safeguards. The objective is to make privacy and targeting intelligence work together, rather than treating them as competing priorities.

Invalid traffic needs to be addressed at multiple points in the advertising lifecycle. Filtering it only after a campaign has run can still result in wasted spend. We therefore use internal invalid traffic detection capabilities at both the pre-bid and post-bid stages.

At the pre-bid stage, the system evaluates available signals and supply characteristics before deciding whether to participate in an auction. This helps reduce exposure to questionable inventory. Post-bid, we analyse delivery and campaign signals to identify patterns that may indicate invalid activity and use these learnings to improve subsequent optimisation.

Fraud detection is also part of our broader machine learning capabilities, alongside audience segmentation, bid optimisation and real-time learning. The objective is to protect both media efficiency and the quality of outcomes.

Inc42: What problem do advertisers still struggle with, and how has Mobavenue built its platform to solve it differently? When did you realise you needed to build more tech in-house?

Tejas Rathod: The fundamental problem advertisers face is not simply acquiring users, but acquiring the right users at the right customer acquisition cost, with a clear path to business value.

We realised early that existing solutions could help us execute media, but they did not give us the level of control and intelligence required to consistently optimise towards the right customer acquisition cost (CAC). That led us to build our tech stack in-house, layer by layer.

Our AI systems analyse billions of signals to identify users with a higher likelihood of conversion, while enabling budgets to be dynamically allocated based on those signals. The objective is not to optimise for media metrics in isolation, but to continuously improve the efficiency and quality of user acquisition. That shift, from media execution to technology-driven outcome optimisation, has been central to how we have built Mobavenue.

Inc42: As brands shift from clicks and installs to outcome-based ROI, how does your engineering team build predictability into the platform? What tech decisions have helped Mobavenue operate at the scale of 1.25 Bn data signals a day?

Tejas Rathod: Predictability starts with the quality and depth of the signals available to the system. Our engineering stack looks at large volumes of consented data signals and combines them with audience segments, behavioural patterns and relevant user attributes to understand intent. 

The objective is not simply to identify a user who may click or install, but to predict the probability of completing the business outcome that the advertiser values.

For example, in a fintech journey, that could extend beyond an app install to KYC completion, investment or loan conversion. Our Neural Network continuously feeds outcomes back into the system, allowing models to learn which signals correlate with quality conversions and improve subsequent decisions.

Adtech is a fast-moving environment where the value of a decision can change within milliseconds, while expectations around accuracy and outcomes continue to increase. So, from the beginning, we made a few deliberate technology choices: real-time decisioning, proprietary intelligence and a common data layer rather than multiple disconnected systems.

The other important decision was to build a closed feedback loop into the platform. Every campaign outcome generates a new learning signal that feeds back into our models, helping improve subsequent decisions around audiences, bidding and budget allocation. 

In FY26, we delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, and this scale of execution gives our models a continually expanding base of learning. For us, maintaining performance at scale means combining speed with continuous learning, so that every decision becomes more informed by the outcomes that came before it.

Inc42: Mobavenue recently formalised its focus on AI infrastructure. How does its Neural Engine think differently from traditional programmatic advertising, and what led you to build an intelligence layer across the marketing lifecycle?

Tejas Rathod: Traditional programmatic advertising is largely designed to make the best decision for the immediate media event, such as whether to bid, how much to bid, or which audience to target. Our Neural Engine is designed to learn from what happens after that decision. We have moved our core decisioning from rule-based and traditional ML systems to a unified neural network architecture built around three stages: process signals, predict intent and produce outcomes.

It continuously processes signals, predicts intent and evaluates downstream outcomes, creating a closed feedback loop where every outcome becomes a new signal for the next decision. So, intelligence does not simply optimise a campaign; it continuously learns what drives quality outcomes and adapts its decisions accordingly.

The adtech ecosystem has become good at automating individual parts of advertising, but intelligence is still fragmented across the marketing lifecycle. Planning, audience selection, campaign execution, creative and reporting often sit across different systems, which means marketers still have to connect the dots and move decisions from one stage to another.

We saw that the next opportunity was not simply to automate another task, but to create an intelligence layer that could continuously connect signals, decisions and outcomes. That thinking led to the Mobavenue Neural Engine. It brings together our proprietary advertising intelligence, first-party platform intelligence and real-time business context to make recommendations that become more relevant as the system learns.

The larger shift is from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across awareness, acquisition and activation. Our Neural Engine is designed to connect planning, execution, optimisation and reporting, while keeping the marketer in control. For us, the future is not just about making advertising faster. It is about making the entire marketing lifecycle more intelligent, connected and outcome-driven.

Inc42: The company closed FY26 with ₹218 Cr+ in revenue and roughly a 20.8% EBITDA margin. How closely do you tie your product roadmap to these metrics, and which products drove the growth?

Tejas Rathod: For us, the product roadmap is primarily driven by the opportunity we see in the market. Financial performance is an important validation, but we do not build products simply around a revenue or EBITDA target. We look at where consumer behaviour, technology and advertiser demand are moving, and then build around those opportunities.

FY26 is a good example of this approach. Our existing platforms, particularly PrsmX and the Neural Engine across all products, were significant contributors to our revenue momentum during the year. These products continued to evolve as we saw greater demand for AI-driven optimisation and outcome-based advertising.

PiiX is the next example of that product philosophy. We identified a significant opportunity in the Apple Search Ads ecosystem and launched PiiX in Q1 FY27 as a dedicated intelligence platform for that high-intent environment. So, the roadmap is driven by market opportunity, while revenue and profitability validate whether we are creating meaningful value from those investments.

Inc42: Over 73% of your revenue now comes directly from brands. What did you change about the platform and reporting to make enterprise clients comfortable managing campaigns directly?

Tejas Rathod: Direct advertiser relationships required us to rethink the platform experience end to end. We undertook a significant overhaul of the interface, underlying infrastructure and reporting capabilities to make the system more robust, intuitive and user-friendly for enterprise teams.

We also expanded the platform’s functionality across campaign planning, execution, creative intelligence and measurement. A key focus was making reporting easier to understand while providing the level of granularity that enterprise advertisers need to evaluate performance, understand where their budgets are being deployed and make informed decisions. 

The objective was to create greater transparency without adding unnecessary complexity. And the larger goal is to make sophisticated technology accessible without requiring the user to deal with the complexity underneath it.

Inc42: How has Mobavenue grown over the past year? Can you share any numbers around campaign performance, advertiser ROI or CAC that highlight the platform’s impact?

Tejas Rathod: Over the past year, our growth has been closely tied to how effectively our technology can improve measurable outcomes for clients. We operate on an outcome-as-a-service model, which means we grow when our clients grow. Revenue per outcome (RPO) is an important business metric for us because it reflects the value generated from every measurable outcome.

Our RPO increased from ₹44.99 in Q1 FY26 to ₹48.44 in Q4 FY26, while quarterly outcomes grew from 9 Mn to 12.61 Mn.

At the campaign level, this translates into measurable performance. Snabbit achieved 5X growth in installs and 10X growth in first-time purchases through precision programmatic optimisation. 

For boAt, our PrsmX platform delivered a 91% view-through rate (VTR), along with a 14% increase in aided awareness, a 20% increase in brand favourability and a 19% increase in purchase intent.

Inc42: Where do you see the next big opportunities for adtech?

Tejas Rathod: I see opportunities across three fundamental areas of brand growth: awareness, acquisition and activation. These are not isolated businesses anymore. A brand may need to create awareness, acquire a user and then activate or retain that user, with intelligence from each stage informing the next. 

That is the direction in which we are building Mobavenue. Our products address these stages, but they are increasingly connected through a common intelligence layer that allows data and learnings to move across the consumer journey.

Inc42: Five years from now, what do you want Mobavenue to be known for?

Tejas Rathod: Five years from now, I would like Mobavenue to be recognised as a technology company that covers the broader digital growth ecosystem, not just advertising. We see significant opportunities across adtech, martech and monetisation technology, and our ambition is to build proprietary platforms across these areas that work together intelligently.

item.title: MeitY Asks Meta To Review Content Recommendation Algorithms
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to…
item.content:encoded:
The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to a limited set of narratives and strengthen checks on content that could cause public disorder or incite violence. 

In an advisory dated October 10, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) directed Meta to provide adequate context for photographs, videos, graphics and other content depicting ongoing public events, particularly when their authenticity, date, location or circumstances may not be readily apparent to users, according to PTI.

The advisory also called for a review of Meta’s recommendation and content-ranking mechanisms to prevent potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material from being disproportionately amplified or repeatedly recommended to users.

“Ensure that recommendation systems do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives, and endeavour to provide appropriate diversity of relevant and credible information,” the advisory said.

It also called for stronger mechanisms to rapidly identify, review and escalate content that gains significant reach through recommendation systems and could potentially cause widespread public confusion, apprehension, violence, or disturbances to public order.

The advisory came amid protests in Delhi by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Similar concerns over content moderation were raised by the government earlier, following a CJP protest at Jantar Mantar in June.

While the advisory does not specify what prompted the government’s move, IT Ministry sources told PTI that agencies had flagged concerns over Meta’s recommendation algorithms, which allegedly appeared to favour certain types of content over others.

What MeitY Wants Meta To Change

The advisory asked Meta to provide users with a diversity of relevant and credible information through its recommendation systems.

It flagged videos, images, statements and graphics relating to public events that were being “prominently displayed and recommended to users” across Meta’s platforms. It warned that such material, when circulated without adequate context or amplified disproportionately, “may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity”.

MeitY asked the company to pay particular attention to old or selectively edited visuals presented as current events, unverified claims about emergencies and police action, and audio-visual material relating to law-and-order situations that lack adequate context. It also called for stronger mechanisms to identify and review content that could incite violence or other unlawful activity.

The advisory invoked the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the IT Rules, 2021, which require intermediaries to exercise due diligence and inform users about prohibited content. It also called for timely cooperation with law enforcement agencies and other authorised government bodies.

Meta was asked to implement the measures “with immediate effect” and inform the ministry of the action taken. The advisory stated that any action must comply with applicable laws while respecting lawful expression and legitimate public discourse.

The directions have drawn criticism from digital rights advocates over its potential implications for freedom of expression and content moderation.

Apar Gupta, founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, described it as a “continuing censorship directive”, arguing that it was not legally binding. Gupta urged MeitY to withdraw the advisory and called on Meta to publicly disclose every takedown and instance of downranking carried out in response to it.

He also questioned the legal basis for the directive, arguing that phrases such as content circulated “without adequate context” and periods of “heightened public-order sensitivity” were not tied to specific provisions of the IT Act or the IT Rules.

item.title: Even Healthcare Raises $50 Mn To Expand Hospital Network Across Bengaluru
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from Alpha Wave.

The all-equity primary round takes its total funding to over $120 Mn, the startup said in a statement.

Even will use the proceeds primarily to expand its hospital network in Bengaluru. It plans to open another hospital by the end of 2026, followed by three more by the end of FY27. It currently operates two multispeciality hospitals on Race Course Road and in HBR Layout.

The startup plans to enter other cities after strengthening its Bengaluru presence. “We want to make sure that Bengaluru patients and members are pretty well served,” cofounder Mayank Banerjee told Inc42.

Even said its valuation had tripled since its previous fundraise 18 months ago, without disclosing its latest valuation. The startup last raised $20 Mn earlier this year to expand its hospital network and launch new facilities.

Founded in 2020 by Banerjee, Matilde Giglio, and Alessandro Ialongo, Even offers an integrated managed care model combining preventive care, outpatient consultations, diagnostics, insurance access, hospitalisation, and post-discharge recovery.

The startup aims to reduce healthcare costs by managing patients’ health beyond individual hospital visits. Its services include telemedicine, at-home blood tests, and medical guidance, alongside cashless hospitalisation through insurance partners.

Even employs salaried doctors whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed or revenue generated. The startup said it assesses doctors on patient outcomes, recovery timelines, and re-admissions.

Banerjee said around 85-90% of Even members living near one of its Bengaluru hospitals choose the startup for their healthcare needs.

Even also uses an AI-based quality system to review cases against clinical protocols in real time. It recently launched Even Spotlight, a dashboard tracking clinical outcomes and patient-reported metrics.

The startup said unplanned re-admissions in programmes run with insurance partners remained below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8-15%. It also claimed average hospital stays were 40% shorter, while proactive care helped more than 200 members avoid hospitalisation, saving an estimated ₹15 Cr to ₹16 Cr.

Even claims to serve more than 2.5 Lakh members across 10 cities, having tripled its membership over the past year.

The hospital expansion follows reports in August that Even laid off around 350 employees as it scaled down its insurance business and shifted resources towards a hospital-led healthcare model. The cuts affected 30-35% of its workforce across multiple teams.

item.content:encoded:
Update| October 19, 17:48

Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 9.92% lower at ₹142.6 apiece on the BSE.

Original| October 19, 12:28 IST

Shares of home services company Urban Company slumped 9.5% to ₹143.30 apiece on the BSE during early trading today, following its Q2 FY27 results and board approval for a fundraise of up to ₹2,500 Cr.

At 12:10 IST, the stock was trading 8.56% lower at ₹144.75 on the BSE. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹22,323 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the time.

Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹182.5 Cr for Q2 FY27 on Friday (October 16) as against a loss of ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier and ₹92.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. 

Operating revenue rose 41% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr, driven largely by higher spending on its quick household help business, InstaHelp.

The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr, including what it described as a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding the vertical, adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹30 Cr. 

The company’s board also approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity shares and/or convertible securities via preferential allotment or private placement.

Urban Company said the proceeds would strengthen InstaHelp’s market leadership, support investment across its three businesses, and fund potential acquisitions.

It is also exploring entry into the residential air conditioner market under its consumer appliances brand ‘Native’, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Management said it could meet its profitability targets without additional capital, although InstaHelp’s losses limited its financial flexibility.

Despite the rise in its loss, Emkay Global Financial Services maintained its ‘Buy’ rating for Urban Company and raised its target price to ₹200 from ₹190, citing growth opportunities across its segments and the strength of its core business.

The brokerage highlighted low penetration of its core services, expansion into Tier II cities, improving international profitability, and the Saudi Arabia business’ progress towards breakeven. It also identified Native as a growth opportunity and said InstaHelp was driving higher customer engagement.

The profit was boosted by an exceptional gain of ₹40.7 Cr from ixigo’s partial exit from electric bus operator Freshbus. In August, ixigo sold a part of its stake in Freshbus for ₹36.6 Cr, bringing its holding down to 8.27% from 25.66%. The gain also included the revaluation of its remaining stake. Following the sale, Freshbus ceased to be an associate of ixigo.

item.title: Zerodha Launches US Stock Investing, Offers Access To 2,000 Stocks
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Discount brokerage Zerodha has launched US stock investing in beta mode on its Kite platform, allowing Indian investors to buy…
item.content:encoded:
Discount brokerage Zerodha has launched US stock investing in beta mode on its Kite platform, allowing Indian investors to buy shares of US-listed companies and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through their existing accounts.

The offering provides access to up to 2,000 US-listed companies and around 1,000 ETFs. It also supports fractional investing, allowing users to invest in a portion of a share with investments starting at $1.

Resident Indian individuals can activate the international investing segment through Kite without opening a separate demat account and transfer funds from their linked Indian bank accounts to a dollar-denominated wallet.

Users can fund their dollar-denominated wallets through netbanking from linked accounts at supported Indian banks. UPI, debit cards, and credit cards are not supported.

Zerodha is charging brokerage of 0.1% of the trade value, subject to a minimum of $0.01 and a maximum of $10 per executed order. An 18% GST applies to brokerage.

Other charges include an IFSCA turnover fee of 0.005% on trade value, along with applicable US regulatory transaction fees on sell orders.

For currency conversion, Zerodha’s guide lists a negotiated bank markup of 0.5%-1.2% over the RBI reference exchange rate.

The service supports delivery-based investing, fractional ownership and SIPs in eligible US stocks. Intraday and margin trading are not available for international equities, and users cannot apply for US IPOs through the platform.

The service is routed through BSE’s India INX Global Access at GIFT City. The underlying US securities are held through a US brokerage partner rather than in an Indian demat account.

Brokers Expand Into US Equities

Zerodha’s launch comes after the startup, along with peers like Groww, Upstoxx and Angel One, received approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) in June to offer investors the option to buy international and US stocks from GIFT City. 

Following this, Groww introduced US stock investing to its customers in September, partnering with US brokerage infrastructure provider Alpaca Securities. Its platform provides access to more than 10,000 US stocks and ETFs and supports fractional investing.

Meanwhile, Upstox launched US stock investing in September, offering access to more than 8,000 US-listed stocks and over 2,000 ETFs, with fractional investments starting at $1.

Earlier today, Angel One also begun rolling out US stock investing on its app to select users, with a wider rollout planned by mid-November. It is offering fractional investing, and will charge zero brokerage till December 2026, post which it will be priced at 0.1% per trade, subject to a minimum of $0.99.

Stockbrokers are diversifying their offerings beyond domestic equities amid a rising demand from Indian retail investors seeking direct exposure to international markets. 

This is driven by a desire to hedge domestic concentration, access global technology megatrends like AI, cloud computing, and semiconductors, and diversify geographical risk, opening up their portfolio to top global companies like NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon. 

The prospect of high-profile US listings, particularly in the technology sector, including companies such as SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, have also drawn investor attention. 

Zerodha and Groww have joined existing providers such as INDmoney and HDFC Securities in providing US investing.
